We conceptualize BZSG as a belief system about the antagonistic nature of social relations--that one person's gain is possible only at the expense of other persons. It appears on a level of personal convictions and as a cultural worldview ideology. We found that persons or nations who believe in a zero-sum game engage in win-lose social exchanges over limited resources. Psychometric evidence for the universality of the BZSG scale in a large pancultural project of 37 nations is presented, where individual and cultural-level predictors of BZSG were tested, followed by their multilevel analyses. BZSG, which shows a conceptual and empirical affinity with societal cynicism, is moderated by previously described cultural dimensions and by objective socio-economic indices. Keywords Belief in a Zero-Sum Game, social axioms, cross-cultural psychology The exploration and identification of universal dimensions of human cultures are the basis of cross-cultural psychology. Values have served as the most popular units of measurement and outcomes in cross-cultural psychology research (Gelfand et al., 2011; Hofstede, 1980; House, Hanges, Javidan, Dorfman, & Gupta, 2004; Inglehart, 1997; Schwartz, 1992; Van de Vliert, 2011). To explain cross-cultural differences and their psychological manifestations, Leung and Bond identified five social axioms at the individual level (Bond, Leung, Au, Tong, & Chemonges- Nielson, 2004; Leung, Au, Huang, Kurman, Nitt, & Nitt, 2007; Leung & Bond, 2004; Leung et al., 2002), which were later reduced to two axioms at the cultural level (Bond, Leung, Au, Tong, De Carrasquel et al., 2004; Leung & Bond, 2008, 2009). However, Leung and Bond suggest that some dimensions of axioms may have been over- looked (Leung et al., 2002). Thus, in this article, we introduce a novel concept, Belief in a Zero- Sum Game (BZSG), which exhibits all the features of an axiomatic belief system, though it has not been found among the five dimensions outlined by the cited authors. The Concept of Social Axioms The field of social axioms refers to the epistemological aspect of culture, in contrast to the axi- ological issue inherent in values (Boski, 2009a). Social axioms have been defined as "general- ized beliefs about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world, which form an assertion about the relationship between two entities or concepts" (Bond, Leung, Au, Tong, De Carrasquel et al., 2004, p. 553; Leung et al., 2002, p. 289). A typical social axiom has the structure "A is related to B," where the relationship may be causal or functional. The concept of a social axiom is different from individual belief domains, which are very specific and appli- cable only to a narrow range of situations and actors. In contrast, social axioms may be viewed as "generalized expectancies," which are highly abstract and related to social behavior across a variety of contexts, targets, and time periods. As Boski and his colleagues have demonstrated, social axioms do indeed possess a structure of general rather than specific or situationally con- strained beliefs: People endorse belief statements of unrestricted character more readily than those confined to specific classes of relationships (Boski, Henne, & Wickowska, 2009). General beliefs were labeled axiomatic because they are often assumed to be true as a result of personal and culturally shared experiences and are transferred through socialization without being questioned (Leung et al., 2002). They serve four major functions: goal attainment (instru- mental), ego defense, value expression, and understanding of the world (Leung & Bond, 2004). Similarly diverse are the domain characteristics of social axioms: psychological attributes (expressing characteristics of individuals), orientation toward the social world (characteristics of groups, organizations, and societies), social interactions (declaring how people interact with each other), and the environment (describing aspects of the environment that have implications for social behavior; Leung et al., 2002). fetched_contents.text: Cultural Values - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. Cultural Values Values may be regarded as socially desirable extrinsic standards, which have been internalized through socialization. Values can also be seen as desired goals and personal preferences when the direct pressure of cultural norms does not prescribe what people can desire or prefer (Vauclair et al., 2105). Values based on extrinsic standards are prescriptive in nature. Vauclair et al. (2015) define prescriptive values as those that individuals feel they should value or are expected to value in their society. Thus, personal values represent intrinsic value motive and prescriptive values extrinsic value motive. Vauclair and her colleagues further suggested that prescriptive cultural values may influence people moral attitudes by restricting tolerance for deviancy, and increasing pressure to conform to culturally accepted ways of think and behave. In the same way, Uz (2015) has differentiated cultures' tightness and looseness. “Tight” cultures have strong norms and a low tolerance of deviant behavior, whereas “loose” cultures have weak norms and a high tolerance of deviant behavior. Thus, feelings of freedom of choice and control as well as tolerance for moral deviations are considered to be psychological symptoms of cultural tightness (Uz, 2015). Cultural tightness can be seen as a synonymous with low-cultural variance and homogeneity. In a heterogeneous culture, norms, values, and standards of behavior are not prescriptive, but in a homogeneous culture, they are pervasive. The article also examines some of the social correlates of values. Values of social collectives representing the cultural level shared values are explored. Examining the research related to shared cultural values, the article suggests the need to look at within cultural variations in values, more specifically examining the differences in values among social and cultural groups so as to have a more nuanced understanding of values in different cultural contexts. Broadly speaking, cultural values shape how people prefer to manage and be managed, as well as their attitudes toward work. Several common frameworks exist for understanding cultural values. Schwartz's (1999) theory of cultural values suggests that all cultures are confronted with three social issues and the institutions developed to resolve these issues impact member values. The first issue is the need to define the nature of the relationship between the individual and the group. How cultures resolve this affects values concerning conservatism, intellectual autonomy, and affective autonomy. The second need is to ensure responsible behavior that will maintain social order. Resolution of this issue influences member values concerning hierarchy and egalitarianism. Finally, cultures must address the relationship between humankind and the natural and social world. The institutions designed to address this need are reflected in mastery and harmony values. Perhaps the most well-known and widely used framework for studying national culture was developed by Geert Hofstede and published in 1980. Hofstede analyzed the values of thousands of IBM employees from dozens of countries and came up with a framework based on four dimensions: individualism–collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity–femininity. Individualism–collectivism reflects the extent to which people prefer to act on their own or as part of a group. In individualistic societies, organizations can expect higher levels of competition and self-interested actions, whereas harmony and loyalty may be the norms in collectivistic societies. Power distance refers to what extent a society accepts the unequal distribution of power. In low power-distance cultures, managers socialize with subordinates and often involve them in decision-making processes. In high power-distance cultures, superior–subordinate relations are very formal; subordinates are expected to obey their superiors without questioning. Uncertainty avoidance reflects the extent to which people feel threatened by situations that are ambiguous or have unknown outcomes and subsequently act to avoid or control such circumstances. In cultures with high uncertainty avoidance, there is a strong preference for formal rules and guidelines; deviance from established behaviors is regarded negatively. In cultures with low uncertainty avoidance, employees are more apt to take risks and be more tolerant of behaviors and opinions that are different from theirs. Hofstede's masculinity–femininity dimension refers to certain sets of values preferred in a society. Masculine societies favor assertiveness, performance, success, money, and materialism. Feminine societies emphasize a friendly environment, job security, cooperation, quality of life, warm personal relationships, and caring for the weak. Masculine cultures are more likely to divide work and social tasks along gender lines, differentiating between jobs meant for men and those meant for women. A recently developed measure of social axioms was validated in a sample of female college students (N=182) from the USA. Five established measures were used to demonstrate convergent validity for the Social Axioms Survey (SAS). The five dimensions of the survey (Control by Fate, Reward for Application, Social Cynicism, Spirituality, and Social Flexibility) were predictably related to the established measures. In addition, a number of self-reported behaviors were also significantly correlated with the social axioms dimensions. While the USA data lend support to the validity of the SAS, validation in other cultures is needed. In addition, the emic aspects of social beliefs in individual cultures should be explored. Introduction Social axioms are generalized statement beliefs about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world. These beliefs are assumed to be true as a result of personal experiences and socialization. Social axioms are central to people’s belief system and improve people’s survival and functioning in their social and physical environment (Lueng, Bond, Reimel de Carrasquel, Yamaguchi, Brierbrauer, & Singelis, in press). In initial studies with five cultural groups, Lueng and his colleagues (in press) developed the Social Axioms Survey (SAS) to identify universal dimensions of culturally related social beliefs. This derived etic measure was shown to comprise five factors or dimensions: Control by Fate, Reward for Application, Social Cynicism, Spirituality, and Social Flexibility (Leung et al., in press). The five dimensions have been used to investigate regional and ethnic variations and its five-factor structure was confirmed in a large USA sample (Singelis et al., submitted for publication). These studies have also demonstrated that while the dimensions seem to be universal, people from different cultures vary in their relative endorsement of the dimensions. The purpose of the current study was to validate the SAS in the USA. First, we will briefly outline the dimensions of culture that have been commonly used in past research. Next, we will discuss the development of social axioms and the importance of social axioms in relation to the values perspective. Finally, we present the current effort to validate the SAS in the USA. Researchers have extensively studied the concept of culture through values. One of the most widely cited systems for describing cultures is Hofstede’s (1980) four-dimensional framework which is based on the work values in 40 countries. Of the four dimensions, individualism–collectivism has been widely used as a theoretical framework in defining culture and detecting cultural variations. In addition to Hofstede’s work, the Chinese Culture Connection (1987) conducted a study based on Eastern values in which they added “Confucian Dynamism” to Hofstede’s four. Another widely recognized system of cultural dimensions comes from Schwartz, 1992, Schwartz, 1994, who researched 41 cultural groups from 39 nations, establishing a mapping of cultures along seven culture-level dimensions of values. Clearly, the values perspective has been influential in defining the ways that researchers compare cultures and explain differences in social behavior, yet there need to be additional dimensions by which we can identify cultures and understand cultural variations. Social axioms have been proposed as an additional framework to complement the values perspective. As mentioned previously, social axioms are generalized beliefs that are used to guide behavior. General beliefs have been related to a variety of social behaviors (e.g. Brody & Shaffer, 1982, Fraser & Gaskell, 1990, Furnham, 1988) and thus, serve well as a complementary framework to values. Moreover, Leung et al. (in press) suggest, “social axioms may provide additional information about cultural variations that may not be explained by the value perspective or they may provide needed triangulation for results stemming from the value perspective” (manuscript p. 4). Social axioms differ from values and other types of beliefs (i.e. normative beliefs). A social axiom proposes a basic premise in the form of an assertion in which a relationship between two entities or concepts is formed. Values assume a form similar to the following statement: “Going to school is important” or “Too much power is bad”. In general, a value states that something is important, desirable or favorable (Leung et al., in press). Conversely, social axioms have two concrete objects such that something is related to something else. For example, “War will lead to the destruction of civilization”. This concreteness should be an advantage in self report data since the statements to which participants react is less abstract and, therefore, more cognitively accessible. Social axioms are defined as generalized beliefs about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world, and they assert the relationship between two entities or concepts [N1-F1]. In other words, social axioms are not simply abstract convictions; they are structured beliefs that claim a relation between two things, such as “A is related to B,” where the relationship may be causal or functional [N1-F1]. This makes them distinct from more specific individual beliefs, because they are broad and abstract, rather than situationally constrained [N1-F1]. The theoretical role of social axioms in cross-cultural studies is to serve as an epistemological framework for culture, complementing the axiological focus of values [N1-F1].

Empirically, social axioms are measured through surveys that operationalize them as generalized statement beliefs. The Social Axioms Survey (SAS) is the most commonly used measure, and it was developed to identify universal dimensions of culturally related social beliefs [N4-F3]. In the initial development, the SAS included five dimensions: Control by Fate, Reward for Application, Social Cynicism, Spirituality, and Social Flexibility [N4-F3]. Later studies confirmed the five-factor structure in a large USA sample and demonstrated that while the dimensions seem universal, cultural differences exist in how they are endorsed [N4-F3]. The evidence also indicates that the SAS was validated in a sample of female college students in the USA and that its convergent validity was supported by correlations with established measures and self-reported behaviors [N4-F3]. The theoretical background further suggests that the SAS is an etic measure, designed to be broadly applicable across cultures [N4-F3].

Cross-culturally, social axioms are most commonly applied in studies comparing cultural groups and investigating how social beliefs vary across societies [N4-F3]. The literature explicitly frames social axioms as a complement to the values perspective, because values are central to cross-cultural psychology and have long been the dominant construct used to compare cultures [N4-F3]. The same source notes that social axioms may provide additional information about cultural variation that is not explained by the values perspective or may serve as needed triangulation for results from the values perspective [N4-F3]. This means social axioms are especially useful when researchers want to explain cross-cultural differences in behavior, attitudes, or organizational outcomes beyond what values alone can account for [N4-F3]. The cited paper also emphasizes that social axioms are useful in explaining cross-cultural differences and similarities in individual behavior [N5-R3]. Overall, social axioms are most commonly applied in cross-cultural contexts where the goal is to uncover broad, culturally shared social beliefs and to understand how those beliefs shape behavior across different groups [N4-F3; N5-R3].

In cross-cultural research, values are defined as desirable goals and guiding principles that are shared among members of a social collective, and they reflect the norms and beliefs that shape behavior [N2-F2]. The cited overview describes values as socially desirable extrinsic standards that have been internalized through socialization, and as desired goals and personal preferences when direct cultural norms do not prescribe them [N2-F2]. It also notes that values can be prescriptive—meaning individuals feel they should value or be expected to value certain things in their society [N2-F2]. The broader cross-cultural perspective presented in the same source identifies several major frameworks for understanding cultural values, including Hofstede’s four dimensions (individualism–collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity–femininity), Schwartz’s seven dimensions, and the GLOBE project’s nine cultural dimensions [N2-F2]. These frameworks are used to compare cultures and explain differences in social behavior [N2-F2].

Normative beliefs, by contrast, are described as preferred patterns of behavior rather than the desirability or importance of an entity or concept [N3-R1]. The excerpt states that values refer to the desirability or importance of an entity or concept, such as power, whereas norms refer to a preferred pattern of behavior [N3-R1]. This distinction is important because values are about what should be valued, while norms are about what should be done [N3-R1]. The broader evidence also indicates that social norms are culturally shaped but are not solely determined by culture; the Quora excerpt notes that social norms, values, and beliefs are influenced by culture and other factors [N3-R5]. In cross-cultural research, normative beliefs are therefore understood as the behavioral expectations that guide how individuals should act in a society [N3-R1; N3-R5].

Values and normative beliefs are related but distinct. Values are prescriptive and represent what is desirable or important; norms are prescriptive and represent what is acceptable or expected behavior [N2-F2; N3-R1]. The overlap between them is that both are culturally embedded and both shape social behavior [N2-F2; N3-R5]. However, they differ in their object of prescription: values prescribe ends or goals, while norms prescribe actions or conduct [N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms, by contrast, are generalized beliefs about how the world functions and how two entities are related [N1-F1]. That means social axioms are more abstract and relational than values and norms, which are more concrete and action-oriented [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. The theoretical background in the shared material also explicitly distinguishes social axioms from values and other types of beliefs, noting that social axioms propose a basic premise in the form of an assertion that two entities or concepts are related, whereas values state that something is important, desirable, or favorable [N4-F3]. This makes social axioms conceptually closer to broad social beliefs than to the narrower categories of values and norms [N4-F3].

In cross-cultural studies, values and normative beliefs are therefore used to understand what cultures prioritize and how they expect people to behave [N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms are used instead when the goal is to understand more general social assumptions and how they shape behavior across contexts [N1-F1; N4-F3]. Because values are tied to desirable ends and norms to acceptable actions, they are especially useful for questions about preferences, goals, and social expectations [N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms are more useful for questions about underlying beliefs about social causality, relationships, and worldviews [N1-F1; N4-F3].

The three constructs—social axioms, values, and normative beliefs—are partially overlapping but are best understood as distinct in concept, even if they are often used together in cross-cultural research [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms are generalized beliefs about how the world functions and how two entities are related [N1-F1]. Values are desirable goals and guiding principles that are shared among members of a social collective [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are preferred patterns of behavior [N3-R1]. These definitions suggest that social axioms are more abstract and relational, values are more prescriptive and goal-oriented, and norms are more prescriptive and action-oriented [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1].

Conceptually, social axioms capture a higher-level epistemological framework for culture, whereas values and norms are more specific and practical. Social axioms are described as “generalized beliefs” that form an assertion about the relationship between two entities or concepts [N1-F1]. Values, by contrast, are defined as socially desirable extrinsic standards and desired goals or preferences [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are defined as preferred patterns of behavior [N3-R1]. This means social axioms are broader in scope than either values or norms; they are not just about what is desirable or what is expected, but about how the social world is structured [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Values and norms, by comparison, are more focused on what should be valued or what should be done [N2-F2; N3-R1].

Each construct captures something the others do not. Social axioms capture underlying social beliefs about relationships and causality, making them especially useful for explaining broad cross-cultural differences in behavior [N1-F1; N4-F3]. Values capture the shared desirable goals and guiding principles of a society, making them especially useful for questions about cultural priorities, preferences, and identity [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs capture the preferred behavioral expectations that guide social conduct, making them especially useful for questions about social expectations, conformity, and appropriate action [N3-R1]. Because of these differences, overlap can cause confusion in cross-cultural studies. For example, a researcher might confuse a social axiom such as “fate controls outcomes” with a value such as “hard work is important,” or with a norm such as “people should behave responsibly” [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Similarly, a researcher might mistake a value-based statement about what should be valued for a normative statement about what should be done [N2-F2; N3-R1]. This overlap is especially problematic when studies use overlapping terms without clearly distinguishing these constructs, because the interpretations and implications of cross-cultural differences can change depending on which concept is being measured [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1].

Each construct is typically operationalized differently in surveys. Social axioms are operationalized as generalized statement beliefs, often through the Social Axioms Survey (SAS), which includes explicit statements that participants endorse [N4-F3]. The SAS was developed to measure five dimensions: Control by Fate, Reward for Application, Social Cynicism, Spirituality, and Social Flexibility [N4-F3]. This operationalization is especially suited to capturing broad, abstract, and relational beliefs about the social world [N1-F1]. Values are operationalized in cross-cultural research through established frameworks and surveys such as Hofstede’s cultural dimensions, Schwartz’s value dimensions, and the GLOBE project’s cultural dimensions [N2-F2]. These frameworks are designed to measure shared desirable goals and guiding principles across cultural groups [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are operationalized as preferred patterns of behavior, and in the available evidence, they are contrasted with values by being described as prescriptive behavioral expectations rather than evaluations of desirability [N3-R1]. The broader evidence also notes that social norms, values, and beliefs are influenced by culture and other factors, which means normative beliefs are often measured through items that ask about acceptable or expected behavior [N3-R5].

Cross-cultural differences are interpreted differently for each construct. For social axioms, differences are interpreted as variation in broad social beliefs and in how people understand the structure of the social world [N1-F1; N4-F3]. The SAS evidence shows that while the dimensions seem universal, people from different cultures vary in how much they endorse them [N4-F3]. For values, cross-cultural differences are interpreted as differences in desirable goals, priorities, and guiding principles, and they are often linked to frameworks such as Hofstede’s, Schwartz’s, or GLOBE’s dimensions [N2-F2]. For normative beliefs, cross-cultural differences are interpreted as differences in acceptable or expected behavior, and they are often tied to social expectations, conformity, and moral attitudes [N3-R1; N3-R5]. Because of this, social axioms are especially useful when researchers want to explain broad cross-cultural differences in behavior that are not fully captured by values alone [N4-F3]. Values are especially useful when researchers want to compare cultural priorities and preferences [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are especially useful when researchers want to understand social expectations and appropriate conduct [N3-R1; N3-R5].

The evidence suggests that each construct is more suitable for certain kinds of cross-cultural questions. Social axioms are most suitable for questions about underlying social beliefs, causal assumptions, and broad worldview differences [N1-F1; N4-F3]. Values are most suitable for questions about cultural priorities, goals, and identity-related preferences [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are most suitable for questions about social expectations, behavior, and conformity [N3-R1; N3-R5]. The shared material also indicates that social axioms are used as a complement to values, because values are central to cross-cultural psychology but may not fully explain cultural variation [N4-F3]. This means social axioms are especially useful for triangulating or extending value-based findings in cross-cultural studies [N4-F3]. Overall, the three constructs differ in both measurement and interpretation, and each is best suited to different kinds of cross-cultural questions depending on whether the focus is on beliefs, goals, or behavior [N4-F3; N2-F2; N3-R1].

## How social axioms are defined in cross-cultural belief studies

In cross-cultural belief studies, **social axioms** are defined as **generalized beliefs** about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world, and they assert the **relationship between two entities or concepts** [N1-F1]. More specifically, social axioms are described as “generalized beliefs about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world, which form an assertion about the relationship between two entities or concepts” [N1-F1]. This makes them fundamentally **relational** and **abstract** rather than situationally specific [N1-F1]. In other words, social axioms are not merely opinions or preferences; they are broad, culturally shared assumptions about how the world works and how people, institutions, or forces interact [N1-F1].

Theoretical role in cross-cultural studies is central. Social axioms are presented as an **epistemological framework** for culture, complementing the **axiological** focus of values [N1-F1]. That means they are used to explain how people understand the structure of social life and how those understandings shape behavior across cultures [N1-F1]. In practice, they are especially useful when researchers want to uncover **universal dimensions of social belief systems** and to explain **cross-cultural differences** in behavior, attitudes, or organizational outcomes that values alone may not fully account for [N4-F3; N5-R3].

## How social axioms differ from values and normative beliefs

### 1) Values

In cross-cultural research, **values** are defined as **desirable goals and guiding principles** that are shared among members of a social collective [N2-F2]. They reflect the norms and beliefs that shape behavior [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that values are socially desirable **extrinsic standards** that have been internalized through socialization, and that they can be seen as **desired goals or personal preferences** when direct cultural norms do not prescribe them [N2-F2]. Importantly, values are prescriptive in nature: individuals feel they should value or be expected to value certain things in their society [N2-F2].

Values are especially useful for questions about **cultural priorities, goals, and identity-related preferences** [N2-F2]. They are also central to cross-cultural psychology because they have long been the dominant construct used to compare cultures [N4-F3]. Common frameworks include Hofstede’s four dimensions, Schwartz’s seven dimensions, and the GLOBE project’s nine cultural dimensions [N2-F2].

### 2) Normative beliefs

**Normative beliefs**, by contrast, are defined as **preferred patterns of behavior** [N3-R1]. The evidence distinguishes them from values by stating that values refer to the **desirability or importance** of an entity or concept, whereas norms refer to a **preferred pattern of behavior** [N3-R1]. In other words, values are about **what should be valued**, while norms are about **what should be done** [N3-R1]. The broader evidence also notes that social norms, values, and beliefs are influenced by culture and other factors, which means normative beliefs are often shaped by both cultural expectations and situational pressures [N3-R5].

Normative beliefs are therefore especially useful for questions about **social expectations, appropriate conduct, conformity, and moral attitudes** [N3-R1; N3-R5].

### 3) How the three constructs relate

Social axioms, values, and normative beliefs are **partially overlapping** but are best understood as **distinct** in concept, even though they are often used together in cross-cultural research [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms are the most abstract and **relational** of the three, because they concern **how the world functions and how two entities are related** [N1-F1]. Values are more **prescriptive and goal-oriented**, because they concern what is desirable or important [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are more **prescriptive and action-oriented**, because they concern what should be done [N3-R1].

The key distinction is that:
- **Social axioms** capture **underlying social beliefs** about structure and causality [N1-F1].
- **Values** capture **shared desirable goals and guiding principles** [N2-F2].
- **Normative beliefs** capture **preferred behavioral expectations** [N3-R1].

Because of this, the three constructs can be thought of as operating at different levels of abstraction and different kinds of prescription: **axioms** are the higher-level beliefs that shape how people understand the social world, **values** are the goals people prioritize, and **normative beliefs** are the rules people follow [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1].

## Main conceptual differences

### What each construct captures that the others do not

1. **Social axioms** capture **underlying social beliefs** about relationships and worldviews [N1-F1]. They are especially useful for explaining broad cross-cultural differences in behavior because they reflect how people understand the social order [N4-F3].
2. **Values** capture **shared desirable goals and guiding principles** [N2-F2]. They are especially useful for comparing cultural priorities and preferences [N2-F2].
3. **Normative beliefs** capture **preferred patterns of behavior** [N3-R1]. They are especially useful for understanding social expectations, conformity, and appropriate action [N3-R1; N3-R5].

### How overlap can cause confusion

Because the three constructs are related, overlap can cause confusion in cross-cultural studies [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. One common source of confusion is that a researcher might mistake a social axiom—such as “fate controls outcomes”—for a value—such as “hard work is important”—or for a normative belief—such as “people should behave responsibly” [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Similarly, a researcher might mistake a value-based statement about what should be valued for a normative statement about what should be done [N2-F2; N3-R1].

This overlap is especially problematic when studies use overlapping terms without clearly distinguishing these constructs, because the **interpretations and implications** of cross-cultural differences can change depending on which concept is being measured [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. For example, a difference in social axiom endorsement may reflect a difference in worldview, while a difference in values may reflect a difference in priorities, and a difference in normative beliefs may reflect a difference in social expectations [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1].

## How they are used cross-culturally

Social axioms are most commonly applied in studies comparing cultural groups and investigating how social beliefs vary across societies [N4-F3]. The evidence explicitly frames them as a complement to the values perspective, because values are central to cross-cultural psychology and have long been the dominant construct used to compare cultures [N4-F3]. The same source notes that social axioms may provide additional information about cultural variation that is not explained by the values perspective or may serve as needed triangulation for results stemming from the values perspective [N4-F3].

Values are most commonly used in cross-cultural research to compare **cultural priorities, goals, and identity-related preferences** [N2-F2]. This is why frameworks such as Hofstede’s, Schwartz’s, and GLOBE’s are so widely used [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are most commonly used to understand **social expectations, behavior, and conformity** [N3-R1; N3-R5].

## Summary

To summarize:

More specifically, social axioms are described as “generalized beliefs about oneself, the social and physical environment, or the spiritual world, which form an assertion about the relationship between two entities or concepts” [N1-F1]. This makes them fundamentally **relational** and **abstract** rather than situationally specific [N1-F1]. In other words, social axioms are not merely opinions or preferences; they are broad, culturally shared assumptions about how the world works and how people, institutions, or forces interact [N1-F1].

That means they are used to explain how people understand the structure of social life and how those understandings shape behavior across cultures [N1-F1]. In practice, they are especially useful when researchers want to uncover **universal dimensions of social belief systems** and to explain **cross-cultural differences** in behavior, attitudes, or organizational outcomes that values alone may not fully account for [N4-F3; N5-R3].

### 1) Values

In cross-cultural research, **values** are defined as **desirable goals and guiding principles** that are shared among members of a social collective [N2-F2]. They reflect the norms and beliefs that shape behavior [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that values are socially desirable **extrinsic standards** that have been internalized through socialization, and that they can be seen as **desired goals or personal preferences** when direct cultural norms do not prescribe them [N2-F2]. Importantly, values are prescriptive in nature: individuals feel they should value or be expected to value certain things in their society [N2-F2].

Values are especially useful for questions about **cultural priorities, goals, and identity-related preferences** [N2-F2]. They are also central to cross-cultural psychology because they have long been the dominant construct used to compare cultures [N4-F3]. Common frameworks include Hofstede’s four dimensions, Schwartz’s seven dimensions, and the GLOBE project’s nine cultural dimensions [N2-F2].

### 2) Normative beliefs

**Normative beliefs**, by contrast, are defined as **preferred patterns of behavior** [N3-R1]. The evidence distinguishes them from values by stating that values refer to the **desirability or importance** of an entity or concept, whereas norms refer to a **preferred pattern of behavior** [N3-R1]. In other words, values are about **what should be valued**, while norms are about **what should be done** [N3-R1]. The broader evidence also notes that social norms, values, and beliefs are influenced by culture and other factors, which means normative beliefs are often shaped by both cultural expectations and situational pressures [N3-R5].

Normative beliefs are therefore especially useful for questions about **social expectations, appropriate conduct, conformity, and moral attitudes** [N3-R1; N3-R5].

Social axioms, values, and normative beliefs are **partially overlapping** but are best understood as **distinct** in concept, even though they are often used together in cross-cultural research [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-R1]. Social axioms are the most abstract and **relational** of the three, because they concern **how the world functions and how two entities are related** [N1-F1]. Values are more **prescriptive and goal-oriented**, because they concern what is desirable or important [N2-F2]. Normative beliefs are more **prescriptive and action-oriented**, because they concern what should be done [N3-R1].

- **Values** capture **shared desirable goals and guiding principles** [N2-F2].
- **Normative beliefs** capture **preferred behavioral expectations** [N3-R1].
